units.title: Unit 1: Ecosystems, Food Webs & Physical Forces

lessons.title: Photosynthesis & How Plants Gain Matter
lessons.reading: Green plants are producers. Using energy from sunlight, leaves combine carbon dioxide from air and water from soil to make sugar and release oxygen. Plants get almost all of their matter from air and water.

principles.title: Photosynthesis and Plant Matter
principles.summary: Plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make food and release oxygen.

bank.prompt: What process do green plants use to make their own food?
bank.explanation: Photosynthesis is the process where plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make sugar.

bank.prompt: Where do plants get the majority of matter to grow?
bank.explanation: Plants build their tissues mostly from carbon dioxide in air and water, not soil.

bank.prompt: Which gas do plants take in from the air during photosynthesis?
bank.explanation: Leaves take in carbon dioxide gas through tiny pores to make plant sugars.

bank.prompt: Which gas do plants release into the air during photosynthesis?
bank.explanation: Plants release oxygen gas as a product of photosynthesis, which animals need to breathe.

bank.prompt: What provides the energy plants need to perform photosynthesis?
bank.explanation: Chlorophyll in green leaves captures energy from sunlight to power photosynthesis.

bank.prompt: What role do green plants play in an ecosystem food web?
bank.explanation: Producers are living things like plants that make their own food using sunlight.

bank.prompt: What are the tiny openings on leaves that exchange gases?
bank.explanation: Stomata are microscopic pores on leaves that let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out.

bank.prompt: What happens to a green plant kept in total darkness?
choices: It cannot make food by photosynthesis
bank.answer: It cannot make food by photosynthesis
bank.explanation: Without light energy, a plant cannot perform photosynthesis to produce sugar.

lessons.title: Food Webs, Consumers & Decomposers
lessons.videoTitle: Khan Academy: Food Chains, Food Webs & Decomposers
lessons.reading: Food webs show how energy and matter move from producers to herbivores, omnivores, and carnivores. Decomposers like fungi and bacteria break down dead material and recycle nutrients back into the soil.

principles.title: Energy Flow and Decomposers in Ecosystems
principles.summary: Energy flows from the Sun to producers and consumers; decomposers recycle matter.

bank.prompt: What do arrows in a food chain show?
choices: The flow of energy and matter
bank.answer: The flow of energy and matter
bank.explanation: An arrow points from the organism being eaten to the organism that gets its energy.

bank.prompt: What do decomposers like fungi and bacteria do in an ecosystem?
choices: Break down dead matter into nutrients
bank.answer: Break down dead matter into nutrients
bank.explanation: Decomposers recycle dead plants and animals back into soil nutrients that plants can use.

bank.prompt: What is an animal that eats only plants called?
bank.explanation: A herbivore is a consumer, such as a rabbit or deer, that eats only plants.

bank.prompt: What is an animal that eats both plants and animals called?
bank.explanation: An omnivore, such as a bear or raccoon, eats both plant and animal matter.

bank.prompt: Where does almost all energy in Earth’s food webs begin?
bank.explanation: Sunlight provides the original energy that producers capture and pass to consumers.

bank.prompt: In Grass → Rabbit → Hawk, what is the rabbit?
bank.explanation: A primary consumer is a herbivore that eats producers like grass.

bank.prompt: Which organism is an example of a decomposer?
bank.explanation: Mushrooms are fungi that act as decomposers by breaking down dead wood and leaves.

bank.prompt: What happens if all decomposers disappear from a forest?
choices: Dead waste piles up and soil loses nutrients
bank.answer: Dead waste piles up and soil loses nutrients
bank.explanation: Without decomposers, nutrients stay locked in dead matter instead of returning to the soil.

lessons.title: Force, Motion, Light & Sound
lessons.videoTitle: Khan Academy: Forces, Motion, Light & Sound Waves
lessons.reading: Greater force causes a bigger change in speed, while heavier objects need more force to accelerate. Light travels in straight lines and can reflect (bounce) or refract (bend). Sound comes from vibrations—faster vibrations make a higher pitch.

principles.title: Force, Mass, Light, and Sound Pitch
principles.summary: Force and mass govern motion; light reflects/refracts and vibration speed sets pitch.

bank.prompt: What happens when a stronger force pushes the same object?
bank.explanation: A greater net force causes a larger change in an object’s motion or speed.

bank.prompt: Which cart speeds up more when pushed with the same force?
bank.explanation: Objects with less mass experience a greater change in motion from the same force.

bank.prompt: How does light travel through air or empty space?
choices: In straight lines until it hits something
bank.answer: In straight lines until it hits something
bank.explanation: Light rays travel in straight lines outward from a source until absorbed, reflected, or refracted.

bank.prompt: What is the bouncing of light off a smooth mirror called?
bank.explanation: Reflection happens when light rays bounce off a surface such as a mirror.

bank.prompt: What is the bending of light as it passes from air into water?
bank.explanation: Refraction is the bending of light when it changes speed moving into a new material.

bank.prompt: What causes all sounds to be produced?
bank.explanation: Sound is produced when an object vibrates back and forth, creating waves in the air.

bank.prompt: How does a faster vibration change the pitch of a sound?
bank.explanation: Pitch is how high or low a sound is; faster vibrations (higher frequency) make higher pitch.

bank.prompt: What force opposes motion when two surfaces rub together?
bank.explanation: Friction is a contact force between rubbing surfaces that slows moving objects down.

units.title: Unit 2: Earth’s Four Spheres & the Solar System

lessons.title: Earth’s Four Spheres & Water Distribution
lessons.videoTitle: Khan Academy: Geosphere, Hydrosphere, Atmosphere & Biosphere
lessons.reading: Earth has four interacting spheres: geosphere (rock/soil), hydrosphere (water/ice), atmosphere (air), and biosphere (living things). About 97% of Earth’s water is salty ocean water, and most freshwater is frozen in glaciers.

principles.title: Earth’s Spheres and Freshwater Distribution
principles.summary: Identify the four Earth spheres and explain where salt and fresh water are stored.

bank.prompt: Which Earth sphere includes all rocks, soil, and mountains?
bank.explanation: The geosphere consists of Earth’s solid rock, soil, landforms, and interior layers.

bank.prompt: Which Earth sphere contains all oceans, rivers, lakes, and glaciers?
bank.explanation: The hydrosphere includes all liquid water, ice, and water vapor on Earth.

bank.prompt: Which Earth sphere is the blanket of gases surrounding the planet?
bank.explanation: The atmosphere is the layer of air (mostly nitrogen and oxygen) around Earth.

bank.prompt: Which Earth sphere includes all living plants, animals, and microbes?
bank.explanation: The biosphere is made up of all living things on land, in water, and in air.

bank.prompt: Where is most of Earth’s water found?
bank.explanation: About 97 percent of Earth’s water is saltwater stored in the oceans.

bank.prompt: Where is the largest amount of Earth’s freshwater stored?
choices: Frozen in glaciers and ice caps
bank.answer: Frozen in glaciers and ice caps
bank.explanation: Most of Earth’s freshwater is frozen solid in glaciers and polar ice caps.

bank.prompt: When a river carves a canyon in rock, which two spheres interact?
bank.explanation: Moving water (hydrosphere) erodes solid rock (geosphere) to carve a canyon.

bank.prompt: Why is most of Earth’s water unavailable for humans to drink?
choices: Most water is salty or frozen
bank.answer: Most water is salty or frozen
bank.explanation: About 97% of water is salty ocean water, and most freshwater is locked in ice.

lessons.title: Solar System, Rotation, Shadows & Orbits
lessons.videoTitle: Khan Academy: Earth’s Rotation, Orbit & Stars
lessons.reading: Earth rotates on its axis every 24 hours to cause day, night, and changing shadow lengths (shortest at noon). Earth orbits the Sun once every 365 days. The Sun looks brighter than other stars because it is much closer to Earth.

principles.title: Earth’s Rotation, Orbit, Gravity, and Star Brightness
principles.summary: Rotation causes day/night; yearly orbit changes seasonal stars; distance affects star brightness.

bank.prompt: What causes the daily cycle of day and night on Earth?
choices: Earth’s yearly orbit around the Sun
The Moon blocking the Sun daily
bank.explanation: Earth spins (rotates) once every 24 hours, causing day on the side facing the Sun.

bank.prompt: How long does it take Earth to complete one orbit around the Sun?
bank.explanation: One full revolution (orbit) of Earth around the Sun takes one year, or about 365 days.

bank.prompt: Why does the Sun look brighter and larger than other stars?
choices: It is much closer to Earth
It is the biggest star in space
Other stars do not make light
bank.answer: It is much closer to Earth
bank.explanation: The Sun is an average-sized star, but it looks brightest because it is closest to Earth.

bank.prompt: In what direction does Earth’s gravity pull objects near the surface?
bank.explanation: Gravity pulls all objects inward toward the center of the planet.

bank.prompt: When is a shadow on the ground shortest during a sunny day?
bank.explanation: At noon the Sun is highest in the sky, casting the shortest shadows.

bank.prompt: Why do we see different constellations in winter than in summer?
choices: Earth orbits to different sides of the Sun
The Sun turns off in winter
bank.answer: Earth orbits to different sides of the Sun
bank.explanation: As Earth revolves around the Sun each year, our night sky faces different parts of space.

bank.prompt: Which object is at the center of our solar system?
bank.explanation: All eight planets, including Earth, orbit the Sun at the center of our solar system.

bank.prompt: Which way does a shadow point when the morning Sun is east?
bank.explanation: Shadows always point away from the light source, so a morning Sun casts shadows westward.

bank.explanation: Most of Earth’s freshwater is frozen solid in glaciers and polar ice caps.

bank.prompt: When a river carves a canyon in rock, which two spheres interact?
bank.explanation: Moving water (hydrosphere) erodes solid rock (geosphere) to carve a canyon.

bank.prompt: Why is most of Earth’s water unavailable for humans to drink?
choices: Most water is salty or frozen
bank.answer: Most water is salty or frozen
bank.explanation: About 97% of water is salty ocean water, and most freshwater is locked in ice.

principles.title: Earth’s Rotation, Orbit, Gravity, and Star Brightness
principles.summary: 24-hour rotation and 365-day orbit create predictable sky patterns.

bank.prompt: What causes the daily cycle of day and night on Earth?
choices: Earth’s yearly orbit around the Sun
The Moon blocking the Sun daily
bank.explanation: Earth spins (rotates) once every 24 hours, causing day on the side facing the Sun.

bank.prompt: How long does it take Earth to complete one orbit around the Sun?
bank.explanation: One full revolution (orbit) of Earth around the Sun takes one year, or about 365 days.

bank.prompt: Why does the Sun look brighter and larger than other stars?
choices: It is much closer to Earth
It is the biggest star in space
Other stars do not make light
bank.answer: It is much closer to Earth
bank.explanation: The Sun is an average-sized star, but it looks brightest because it is closest to Earth.

bank.prompt: In what direction does Earth’s gravity pull objects near the surface?
bank.explanation: Gravity pulls all objects inward toward the center of the planet.

bank.prompt: When is a shadow on the ground shortest during a sunny day?
bank.explanation: At noon the Sun is highest in the sky, casting the shortest shadows.

bank.prompt: Why do we see different constellations in winter than in summer?
choices: Earth orbits to different sides of the Sun
The Sun turns off in winter
bank.answer: Earth orbits to different sides of the Sun
bank.explanation: As Earth revolves around the Sun each year, our night sky faces different parts of space.

bank.prompt: Which object is at the center of our solar system?
bank.explanation: All eight planets, including Earth, orbit the Sun at the center of our solar system.

bank.prompt: Which way does a shadow point when the morning Sun is east?
bank.explanation: Shadows always point away from the light source, so a morning Sun casts shadows westward.
